narrative:
The model determined that you have an 80% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven first by your class ranking at the end of your third year, which placed you in the second decile—well below the average of accepted students. This was the single strongest factor pulling the prediction toward failure. Your first-year ranking in the second decile had the next largest impact, again pointing the model toward a likely bar exam failure. Finally, your undergraduate GPA of 2.80, noticeably lower than the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, added further weight in the same direction.

All three of these academic performance signals told the model you would struggle with the bar exam, and none of your other characteristics—such as your LSAT score being only slightly below average, your middle-income background, being male, white, or planning to attend full-time—were strong enough to offset that outlook.

What you should do next is focus on improving your academic trajectory. Raising your grades sharply in the remaining years, seeking targeted bar-prep support, or retaking courses to strengthen core skills could meaningfully change your profile before you reapply.
